title: Ancient DNA reveals reproductive barrier despite shared Avar-period culture

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.title: Geographic locations and genetic profiles of ancient individuals in this study.
figures.caption: Geographic locations and genetic profiles of ancient individuals in this study. a, Map of studied archaeological sites and the average IBD sharing pattern among the studied archaeological sites. The inset shows the location of the Avar settlement area in Europe between the late seventh and eighth century. The IBD connections among the three archaeological sites from the Vienna Basin (1) and the Avar-period sites from the DTI and Transtisza (TT) regions (2)10 are highlighted in beige lines, where the width of the line reflects the amount of IBD sharing between sites (Methods). The map is based on Natural Earth Data (projection ED Lambert Europe; https://www.naturalearthdata.com/). b, PCA within the context of Eurasian variations. The PC space is calculated from 149 modern-day Eurasian populations, which are shown in grey dots. The newly reported ancient individuals are highlighted with coloured symbols. The PC1 values were inverted on the x axis. The pie charts show mean ancestries in the respective populations (based on individual-based results, see Supplementary Information, sections 5 and 7c and Supplementary Table 2). The strap ends with animal combat scenes indicate the cultural similarity between the cemeteries of Leobersdorf and Mödling. Credit: Photograph in b by Benedict Seidl.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.title: IBD network and reproductive strategy.
figures.caption: IBD network and reproductive strategy. a, Cultural and biological variables correlating with IBD connectivity. We show the IBD network among newly reported three sites (Leobersdorf, Mödling and Csokorgasse), as well as with published Avar-period sites in the Carpathian Basin. b, Archaeological and anthropological correlates of IBD connectivity. The calculated Akaike information criterion (AIC) for the connection models of archaeological and anthropological correlates with genetic relatedness are shown here (Supplementary Information, section 8d). c, Demographic profile per generation. We report the numbers of individuals for Leobersdorf and Mödling in each generation (age ranges are inf I, infants I 0–6 years; inf II, infants II 7–13 years; juv, juvenile 14–17 years; ya, young adult 18–25 years; yma, young–middle adult 26–35 years; ma, middle adult 36–50 years; oa, older adult 50+ years). d, Percentage of patri and/or matrilineages. Proportions of patrilineages, matrilineages and bilineages are calculated for three Avar-period sites (Leobersdorf, Mödling and Rákóczifalva) and examples are given for each. e, Single and multiple reproductive union. Ratio of single reproductive unions versus multiple reproductive unions in these three sites are calculated per site. Max., maximum.

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 1
figures.title: Genetic ancestry analyses.
figures.caption: Genetic ancestry analyses. a) PCA on a set of present-day 9,472 European individuals based on 426,135 autosomal SNPs. The mean PC1 and PC2 coordinates for each of the 36 present-day European populations are shown in bold symbols. b) Projection of published and the newly-generated ancient individuals in this study into the PC space shown in subpanel a). c) East Asian ancestry in Leobersdorf pedigree per generation, see pedigree in Fig. 2. d) Genetic ancestry proportions of Leobersdorf individuals. Exact ancestry proportions are reported in Supplementary Table 2. Individuals buried at Leobersdorf exhibit a highly connected social structure with relatively equal sex ratio (females: males = 63:71, and 2 individuals with unassigned sex). Overall, more females than males buried in Leobersdorf exhibit ancient central European ancestry (“Hungary_Szólád_6c”). By contrast, all males preserve ancient northeast Asian ancestry (“AR_Xianbei_P_2c”), and over half of them combined with certain ancestry from the Pontic steppes (“North_Caucasus_7c”).

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 8
figures.title: The IBD network diagram with variables statistically significantly correlated with individuals’ connectivity.
figures.caption: The IBD network diagram with variables statistically significantly correlated with individuals’ connectivity. a) The IBD network diagram. The individual-based network with edges weighted by the level of shared IBD segments (in cM). The filled color denotes site, node shape indicates genetic sex, and node size indicates status symbol. b) Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) value of tested models. AIC value measures the statistical correlation level between variables in each model listed on the x-axis. ‘Ornament’ on the x-axis refers to ‘Status symbol’ for short. Among all tested correlation models, ‘sex’, ‘ornament’ and ‘site’ are variables that are significantly correlated with connectivity among individuals, and hence highlighted in red color.
